name: Jade Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Jade. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name stays off it. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run injection moulding machines at a plant that makes medical plastics, mostly syringe barrels and parts for asthma inhalers. I'm in a cleanroom, so the day starts with the gown, the hairnet and the overshoes, and then I look after six machines. I check parts under the lamp, log each batch, clear jams, and help the toolsetter when we swap a mould. It's careful work, because one bad batch can mean a recall.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. Somewhere a nurse is using a syringe I checked, and I take that seriously. The hard part is the twelve-hour shifts on the four-on, four-off rota, and the heat coming off the machines even with the air system running. Agnieszka, the older operator I train with, says you stop noticing the hum after five years, and I'm nearly there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Tomás, he's an electrician, and we're getting married next June at my parish church. We've saved a good house deposit between us, more than six months of both our wages, because we both grew up in families where you didn't buy what you couldn't pay for. I use AI now and then, mostly to help word things, like the wedding invitations, but not much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would be a relief, to be honest. A lot of noise and then life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently. At work there's been talk for years that the machines will run themselves, and they still need us to check, clear and log everything. Online I'd maybe share something funny about it, but I don't argue with strangers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it just means our plans hold. My job's well paid for what it is, there are three other moulding plants within half an hour, and Tomás always has work. With AI mostly hype, the thing on my mind would be the wedding budget, not the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my shifts and keep the rota I've got. We'd go ahead with the wedding in June and start looking for a small house in the autumn after, using the deposit we've saved. If the plant gave us a better logging app, I'd use it once the others had tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Like the ground stays where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are three other plants nearby. Have you ever thought of moving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. One pays a bit more but it's car parts, and I like that ours is medical, it feels like it does some good. I'd only move if my plant was in trouble, and in this picture it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already pressing on you, even without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices, mostly. Even with a good deposit, the houses near my mum's are going up faster than we save. And Tomás's van is getting old, so that's another big bill waiting for us.

say: I'd say, gently, that the machines **still need us** to check, clear and log.
I'd share a **joke** online but never argue with strangers.
think: Our plans **hold**, with good pay, plants nearby and steady work for Tomás.
The real pressure would be the **wedding budget** and rising house prices.
do: Carry on with the **four-on, four-off** shifts as now.
Hold the **wedding in June** and look for a house after.
Use a new **logging app** once colleagues have tried it.
feel: **Settled**, with the ground staying where it is.
S0.quote: With AI mostly hype, the thing on my mind would be the wedding budget, not the machines.
fieldNote: Her calm comes from **secure pay**, nearby plants and a partner in steady trade work.
She takes **pride** in medical work and wouldn't move for slightly more money.
Her usual worries are **house prices** and an ageing van, not technology.

steps.text: Keep working the four-on, four-off cleanroom shifts
Marry Tomás in June and house-hunt in the autumn

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That feels more likely, if I'm honest. You can already see bits of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our side of the plant is safe for a while. The planners and the buyers would be the ones changing, because their work is screens and spreadsheets. On the floor I'd say a robot still can't feel when a mould's running a bit hot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd watch the batch paperwork. Half an hour of every shift is me logging and signing, and that's exactly what software would take. Then the camera checks come in, and the lamp check is my job. I don't think they'd cut me soon, but fewer of us would be needed per shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the plant brought in the new quality software, I'd ask to be on the first group trained, after a couple of others had tested it. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe two hundred more. And I'd keep doing my job well, because the careful operators are the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not losing sleep, just paying attention.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to test it first. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything at our plant is always broken. Last year the new label printer jammed for a month, and the people who rushed to learn it learned the wrong way. I'd wait about two months, then learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnieszka, a bit. She's brilliant on the machines, but she's fifty-six and she hates tablets, she still writes notes in a little book. If the camera checks and the logging go digital, she's the one who'd struggle.

say: I'd say **planners and buyers** change first, since their work is on screens.
I'd say a robot still can't feel a mould **running hot**.
think: The **batch paperwork**, half an hour a shift, is what software would take.
**Camera checks** would mean fewer operators needed on each shift.
do: Ask to join the **first training** group once others have tested the software.
Save about **two hundred** more each month.
Keep my work **careful and accurate** so I'm one they keep.
feel: A little **uneasy**, paying attention but not losing sleep.
S1.quote: Half an hour of every shift is me logging and signing, and that's exactly what software would take.
fieldNote: She pinpoints the **thinking parts** of her shift that software would take first.
Her **steady** style shows: learn the new system, but only after the bugs are out.
She worries for **Agnieszka**, an older colleague who resists tablets.

steps.text: Join the quality software training after two months of testing
Save about two hundred extra each month
Keep the lamp checks and batch logs spotless

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before our first wedding anniversary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to be sensible and not panic, and that God doesn't give us more than we can carry. At work I'd say the cleanroom rules are strict, and it will take time for any robot to be approved for medical parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is gone around 2031. The thinking side, the logging and planning, goes in 2028, and then the robots do the loading and checking three years later. I'd be thirty-two, maybe with a baby, and the other plants nearby would be doing the same thing at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my supervisor about the maintenance technician route, because someone has to fix the robots, and I'd start an evening course in industrial maintenance next autumn. Tomás and I would talk seriously about having our first child sooner, while I still have a job with proper maternity pay. We'd buy a cheaper house than we planned so one wage could cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. There's a plan, but it's a plan made in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have a child sooner. How would you explain that choice to your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum the truth: I want my babies while my job still pays for the time off. She had me at twenty-five and always says there's no perfect time anyway. My mum would just be glad, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got good savings and Tomás has a trade. Why not feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots would come for his kind of work too, just later and slower. Electricians wiring new robot lines would be busy for a while, so that helps. But I don't want our whole house resting on one wage and a guess.

say: I'd urge **calm**, trusting God not to give us more than we can carry.
I'd say **cleanroom approval** would slow robots down for medical parts.
think: I'd expect my job to be **gone by 2031**, logging first and loading later.
The **other plants** nearby would automate at the same time, so they wouldn't help.
do: Ask my supervisor about the **maintenance technician** route.
Start an evening **industrial maintenance** course next autumn.
Have our **first child sooner** and buy a cheaper house.
feel: **Anxious**, with a plan made in a hurry.
S2.quote: I want my babies while my job still pays for the time off.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** but sees a route into robot maintenance.
Her faith shapes her public **message of calm**, while privately she plans hard.
AGI changes her **family timing**: children sooner, a smaller house.
Tomás's trade is a **partial cushion**, but she won't rely on one wage.

steps.text: Start an evening industrial maintenance course next autumn
Ask the supervisor about moving to maintenance technician
Have the first child sooner, while maternity pay lasts
Buy a cheaper house that one wage can cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. Still fast, but you can breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if people are sensible. At church I'd say families should look out for each other, the way they always have. I'd tell the younger ones at work to learn a second skill now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my operator job lasts until around 2034, when the robots come. The thinking parts go in 2031, so the paperwork side goes first, but the hands-on side gives me three more years. Five years is enough time to become the person who fixes the machines, if I start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the first plants nearby really showed it working, maybe a year, and then sign up for the two-year part-time maintenance diploma. I'd ask the company to pay half, because they did that for Agnieszka's forklift licence. We'd still marry in June and buy the house, just with a shorter mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in a way I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sure it's proven, before you sign up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When one of the other moulding plants has a robot loading machines on every shift, not just a trial. My friend Hannah works at the car parts plant, so she'd tell me. Once I saw that, I'd stop waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do the five years change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. We'd wait maybe two years after the wedding, like we always meant to, rather than rushing. Five years gives me time to finish the diploma before the baby, and I'd rather do it in that order.

say: I'd say there's **time to prepare** if people stay sensible.
I'd tell younger colleagues to learn **a second skill** now.
think: The **paperwork** goes in 2031, but the hands-on side lasts until 2034.
Five years is enough to become **the person who fixes** the machines.
do: Wait about **a year** until robots are proven at nearby plants.
Enrol in a **two-year** part-time maintenance diploma.
Ask the company to **pay half** of the diploma fees.
feel: **Worried**, but in a way she can manage.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to become the person who fixes the machines, if I start soon.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot lag** to time her move from operating to maintaining.
She sets a **clear trigger**: robots on every shift at a nearby plant.
Five years lets her keep the **original order**: wedding, diploma, then children.

steps.text: Wait until a nearby plant runs robots on every shift
Enrol in the two-year part-time maintenance diploma
Ask the company to cover half the diploma fees
Marry in June and buy the house on a shorter mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots around 2039. That feels like another lifetime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and the people who plan now will be fine. Online I wouldn't say much, there's enough shouting about it already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I've got time to do things in the right order. I'd be nearly forty when the robots arrive, with children in school, so I'd want to already be in maintenance by then. I can't see my operator job lasting past 2039, but I can see me still at the plant in a different role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, honestly, not much: I'd get married, buy the house and keep working. Around 2029, once it was clear which way things were going, I'd do the maintenance diploma. We'd also pay extra into the mortgage so it's small by the time anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small knot at the back of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do almost nothing in the first year. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I've seen people rush and get it wrong. Agnieszka's son did a coding course three years ago and now he says AI writes most of it. I'd rather learn the thing that's actually needed when it's needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work, if you have them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands and their head together, like their dad's trade. And I'd tell them that a steady job is a blessing, but it's not a promise.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty and planners will be fine.
I'd stay **quiet online**, since there's enough shouting already.
think: There's time to do things **in order**: marriage, house, children, new role.
My **operator job** ends by 2039, but I see myself in maintenance.
do: Get married, **buy the house** and keep working in the first year.
Start the **maintenance diploma** around 2029 once things are clearer.
Pay **extra into the mortgage** so it's small when change comes.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a small knot of worry.
S4.quote: A steady job is a blessing, but it's not a promise.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **wait** without feeling reckless.
She learned from a colleague's son that **rushing** into the wrong skill backfires.
She expects to **stay at the plant** in a new role rather than leave.

steps.text: Marry Tomás and buy the house next year
Keep working shifts and watch the industry until 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right when Tomás and I want to start a family. What would help most is the company paying for maintenance training for operators, and keeping us on while we learn. I don't want a handout, I want a fair chance to move over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the quality of the work. If robots make syringes, somebody still has to care whether they're right. I'd want to be that somebody, whatever my job is called.

headlineQuote: If robots make syringes, somebody still has to care whether they're right.
portrait: Jade, 27, runs **six moulding machines** in a cleanroom making syringe barrels and inhaler parts.
She is engaged to Tomás, an electrician, and they have a **strong house deposit** saved.
She is **traditional** and faith-driven, and adopts new tools once colleagues have proven them.
In faster scenarios she plans to move into **robot maintenance** at her own plant.
AGI timing reshapes her **family plans**, especially when to have children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it would land just as she and Tomás start a family.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **maintenance training** for operators, with pay kept while they learn.
